title: Beechcraft Baron 58 — Emergency Procedures
description: Emergency procedures for the Beechcraft Baron 58 with twin Continental IO-550 fuel-injected engines, constant-speed propellers, and retractable tricycle gear. Memory items are marked. The Baron has counter-rotating propellers which reduce P-factor at cruise power, but VMC considerations and single-engine climb performance are critical — review per POH before each flight. All airspeeds, power settings, and numerical limits must come from the specific aircraft POH. The IO-550 is fuel-injected; carburetor icing is not applicable. This file does not substitute for recurrent emergency training, simulator practice, or a Baron type-specific checkout with a qualified instructor.

source.notes: No manufacturer document consulted. Written from general familiarity with the type.

known_issues.description: Contains no airspeeds, power settings, fuel quantities, or other numerical limitations — all must come from the specific aircraft POH.
Equipment variations exist across Baron 58 airframes. Verify every item against the specific aircraft and its POH before use.

rights.notes: Manufacturer POH remains under copyright. This file does not reproduce its wording or selection of items.

sections.title: Engine Failure on Takeoff — Before or At Liftoff

items.text: Throttles — both
Brakes — apply firmly to stop within remaining runway
Mixtures — both
Ignition switches — both
Fuel selectors — both
Master switch

In a light twin, a turnback to the runway after an engine failure at low speed and altitude is rarely survivable. If airborne with insufficient runway remaining, land straight ahead or within a narrow arc on the best available surface.
Occupants — advise to brace for impact if a ground roll stop is not possible

sections.title: Engine Failure in Flight — Identify / Verify / Feather / Secure

items.text: The identify-verify-feather-secure sequence is fundamental to twin-engine operations. Dead foot = dead engine: the failed engine is on the same side as the foot that is not pressing the rudder. Confirm before feathering.
Airspeed — immediately establish and maintain at or above Vmc; target Vyse (blue line) to optimise climb or minimise sink
items.response: AT OR ABOVE VMC; TARGETING VYSE PER POH

items.text: Identify failed engine — note which foot is applying rudder to maintain directional control; failed engine is on the same side as the idle rudder foot
Verify failed engine — retard the suspect throttle slightly; confirm no change in power or yaw tendency
Failed engine propeller — feather by pulling the failed engine's propeller control to the FEATHER detent
Bank toward operating engine — establish a shallow bank per POH toward the good engine to assist rudder in maintaining directional control
Failed engine fuel selector
Failed engine mixture
Failed engine ignition switch
Failed engine boost pump
Operating engine — verify full power; fuel selector, mixture, boost pump, and magnetos on
items.response: FULL POWER; ALL SYSTEMS CONFIRMED ON

items.text: Drag — landing gear up, flaps up, failed engine cowl flap closed
Altitude and terrain — assess single-engine climb or descent capability versus terrain and obstacle clearance
items.response: TERRAIN CLEARANCE CONFIRMED OR LANDING AREA SELECTED

items.text: Squawk and declare — transponder 7700; advise ATC of engine failure and intentions
Airspeed — pitch immediately to maintain Vmc or above; Vyse (blue line) is the target climb speed
items.response: AT OR ABOVE VMC; VYSE PER POH

items.text: Identify failed engine — dead foot / dead engine
Failed engine — complete the identify / verify / feather / secure sequence
Landing gear — retract if not already up
Flaps — retract if extended
Single-engine climb — if terrain and performance permit, continue to a safe altitude for return and landing; otherwise land ahead
ATC — advise of emergency; request priority handling
Affected engine throttle
Affected engine mixture
Affected engine fuel selector
Affected engine propeller
Affected engine ignition switch
Affected engine boost pump
Airspeed — increase if fire persists; airflow may help extinguish or carry flame away from airframe
items.response: AIRSPEED INCREASED PER POH IF FIRE CONTINUES

items.text: If fire extinguishes — secure engine; proceed to nearest suitable airport; advise ATC
If fire does not extinguish — prepare for emergency landing; squawk 7700; brief occupants to brace
Throttle — affected engine
Mixture — affected engine
Fuel selector — affected engine
Ignition switch — affected engine
Master switch
Fuel selectors — all remaining
Occupants — evacuate via pilot door and cabin entry door; move upwind of aircraft
Fire extinguisher — if available and fire is small, discharge through cowling openings from upwind
Emergency services — call for assistance; do not re-enter the aircraft
Master switch
Avionics master switch
All electrical switches — switch off individually to isolate the source
Vents and fresh air — open pilot air vents to clear smoke from cockpit
If fire is out and source is isolated — leave offending circuit off; restore minimum essential electrical power
Land as soon as practicable — declare emergency; advise ATC
Oil pressure gauge — verify low reading and cross-check oil temperature for a corroborating rise
items.response: LOW PRESSURE CONFIRMED; OIL TEMP TREND NOTED

items.text: Affected engine power — reduce to minimum required to maintain level flight or a controlled descent
Land as soon as possible — a confirmed zero oil-pressure reading means engine failure is imminent; do not delay
If engine seizes or fails — execute identify / verify / feather / secure sequence
ATC — advise of emergency and intentions; request priority handling
Airspeed — establish best glide speed per POH to maximise glide range
Landing area — choose the best available field, road, or surface within gliding distance; commit early
Mayday — squawk 7700; transmit position and situation on 121.5 MHz or last assigned frequency
Restart attempt — if altitude permits, attempt restart per engine-failure-in-flight checklist
Fuel selectors — both
Mixtures — both
Ignition switches — both
Master switch — leave on until flaps are set and gear decision is made, then off
Landing gear — extend if a prepared surface is assured; consider gear-up for soft field or obstacle clearance
items.response: DOWN (HARD SURFACE) OR UP (SOFT OR OBSTACLE) PER CONDITIONS

items.text: Seat belts and shoulder harnesses — all occupants
Doors — crack open to prevent jamming on impact
Airspeed — reduce to gear extension speed range; avoid overstressing gear doors
items.response: BELOW GEAR EXTENSION SPEED PER POH

items.text: Landing gear handle — cycle up then down; allow full travel and listen for gear actuation
Gear circuit breaker — check that gear system breaker is not tripped; reset once if tripped
If normal extension fails — proceed to emergency gear extension checklist
ATC — advise of gear problem; request low pass for tower gear verification if available
Airspeed — reduce to gear extension speed or below per POH before activating emergency system
items.response: BELOW GEAR EXTENSION SPEED PER POH

items.text: Gear handle
Emergency gear extension handle or CO2 lever — locate and activate per POH procedure
Gear-down indication — verify three green lights illuminate after extension
If only partial indication — assume unsafe; advise ATC; consider belly landing or gear-up landing
After an emergency gear extension, retraction is generally not possible. Plan for landing at the nearest suitable airport.
Failed engine — confirm feathered and secured before initiating approach
Operating engine — full power available; mixture rich, fuel selector on best tank, boost pump on, magnetos on BOTH
Airspeed — fly approach at single-engine approach speed per POH; higher than normal approach speed accounts for reduced go-around margin
Flap extension — use minimum flap consistent with field length; excess flap dramatically degrades single-engine go-around performance
items.response: MINIMUM NECESSARY FLAP PER CONDITIONS AND POH

items.text: Landing gear — extend when landing is assured; delay as long as practical to preserve single-engine go-around option
Stabilise early — single-engine approaches require a long, stable final; do not attempt a steep or rushed approach
ATC — advise of single-engine approach; request emergency services standing by
Plan to land long if uncertain — it is better to roll off the far end than to attempt a go-around from too low or too slow
An engine-out go-around is extremely hazardous at low altitude. Commit to landing whenever possible. Initiate only if a safe landing cannot be made and climb performance is assured.
Operating engine — full power immediately; smooth application to avoid loss of directional control
Pitch — immediately establish climb attitude; maintain Vyse (blue line) per POH; remain above Vmc
items.response: VYSE ATTITUDE; AIRSPEED AT OR ABOVE VMC

items.text: Rudder — full rudder toward operating engine; use all available rudder to counter yaw
Flaps — retract to takeoff position immediately on first increment
Landing gear — retract after positive climb is established
Flaps — retract fully after obstacle clearance and positive climb confirmed
ATC — advise of engine-out go-around; declare emergency if not already declared
